frase_gancho.texto: Mexico’s most famous stone is not a calendar.

puente_narrativo.texto: With it, the Mexica Hall comes to an end. Next comes the Oaxaca Hall: there, centuries before Tenochtitlan existed, the Zapotec flattened a mountain to found Monte Albán, and they were already praying to Cocijo, the Oaxacan brother of Tláloc.

guion_corto.texto: You are standing in front of the Sun Stone, a basalt disc more than three and a half meters in diameter that weighs nearly twenty-five metric tons. It is called the “Aztec calendar,” but it was not used to tell the date: it is a sacred monument that tells how the world we live in was born. At the center is the face of Tonatiuh, the Sun, with his tongue shaped like a flint knife. Around it, in four panels, appear the four previous suns, destroyed one after another. Farther out there is a ring with the twenty day signs and, along the edge, two fire serpents that seem to guide the Sun across the sky. It was carved toward the end of the empire and was found in 1790.

guion_largo.texto:
Let’s start with what it is not. Although everyone calls it the “Aztec calendar,” the Mexica did not use it to know what day it was. They had calendars in abundance, painted in codices, and this stone is not practical: it weighs almost twenty-five metric tons and it lay flat on the ground. It is something else: a map of time and destiny. It tells where the world comes from, how long it will last, and what must be done so that it does not come to an end.

Look at the center. There is Tonatiuh, the Sun, his face full of strength and his tongue stuck out, turned into a flint knife. On either side, two claws hold human hearts. Do you remember the [Disc of Death](mna_s04_disco_muerte) from Teotihuacán, with its knife tongue? It is the same idea: the Sun is hungry, and it must be fed. Around the face the sign Nahui Ollin takes shape, “Four Movement.” It was the name of the Fifth Sun, ours, and also the sign of its end, because it was expected to end in earthquakes.

In the four arms of that sign are the four previous suns. According to the creation myths, the first, the Jaguar Sun, ended when wild beasts devoured the humans. The second, the Wind Sun, ended in hurricanes, and the people turned into monkeys, like the one on the obsidian vessel. The third, the Fire Rain Sun, ended under a fire that fell from the sky, and the people turned into birds. The fourth, the Water Sun, presided over by the goddess [Chalchiuhtlicue](mna_s04_chalchiuhtlicue), the one from the Teotihuacán monolith, ended in a flood, and the people turned into fish. Four worlds, four failures. The Mexica lived in the fifth, and they knew that it, too, could come to an end.

The Fifth Sun, according to the legend you already know, was born in Teotihuacán, when the poor, sick god Nanahuatzin threw himself into the fire. But the Sun did not move until the gods sacrificed themselves. That is why humans had to repay them with offerings, with blood and hearts. It was not cruelty for its own sake; it was a kind of cosmic contract: the Sun gives you life, and you give it what you have.

Farther out turns the ring of the twenty day signs, from Cipactli, the primordial crocodile, to Xóchitl, the flower. Look for them: somewhere there is a monkey, ozomatli, the same as the one on the obsidian vessel you saw a moment ago, and the flower of [Xochipilli](mna_s06_xochipilli). On the outer edge, two fire serpents, Xiuhcóatl, the weapon with which Huitzilopochtli defeated [Coyolxauhqui](mna_s06_coyolxauhqui) in the myth. Their tails meet at the top, next to the sign 13 Reed, which many connect with the birth of the Fifth Sun. Their heads meet at the bottom, and two faces peer out from their jaws.

When was it made? That is debated. Some date it to the time of King Axayácatl, around 1479; others, to that of Moctezuma Xocoyotzin, around 1512. In any case, it comes from the last decades of the empire. The block of basalt is thought to have come from the south of the valley, from the lava field of the Xitle volcano, the same one that buried Cuicuilco, the circular pyramid you saw in the model, in the hall of the first villages. A stone born of an eruption that had already buried a city.

Today you see it gray, but five centuries ago it was painted, in red and ocher, among other colors. Imagine the effect: a colored disc, lying on the ground, under the open sky of Tenochtitlan.

Its modern history reads like a novel. After the conquest it was left buried beneath the Main Plaza, until December 17, 1790, when workers who were leveling and paving the plaza came across it. A year later, in the same spot, the [Stone of Tízoc](mna_s06_tizoc) appeared. The Sun Stone was set upright on the west tower of the Cathedral, in plain view of everyone, until in 1885 it was taken to the National Museum, on Moneda Street. And in June 1964 it made its last journey, to Chapultepec. Shortly before, the giant Tláloc that you saw at the entrance had made the same trip. 1964 was the year of the great moves.

And when you say goodbye to it, think that, for the Mexica, the world had already ended four times and nothing was guaranteed. Perhaps that is why they took such care over every detail of their cosmos: if everything can end, everything deserves to be named.

texto: Look for the knife tongue on the face at the center
Find the twenty day signs: can you spot the monkey and the flower?
Circle the stone with your eyes and locate the two fire serpents

texto.Material: Olivine basalt with red and ochre pigments
texto.Dimensions: 358 cm in diameter x 98 cm thick

texto.pregunta: Myth: The Sun Stone was the calendar the Mexica used to know the date.
texto.respuesta: Reality: It was not a calendar for daily use. It is a ceremonial monument, made to lie flat on the ground, that sums up how the Mexica understood time and the destiny of the world.
